transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-11 16:00 PT | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (BlueRiver - ML Platform), Marcus Green (BlueRiver - Infra), Eloise Tan (Product), Tom O'Riley (SRE)
Recording: https://redwood-recordings.s3/ff/ff-20260611-9f3b.mp3

Summary: Quick status check on Dedicated sizing and autoscale guardrails. Run a targeted burst simulation to validate warm-pool / pre-warm behavior; reconcile cost vs latency tradeoffs; confirm instrumentation and alerting for canary/fallback policy.

Topics: Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policy thresholds, warm pool / pre-warm, burst simulation plan, KV cache warming, fallback to quantized model variant, SLO headroom, cost projection

Transcript:
00:00 Sara Kim: all right everyone thanks for joining, uh we've got 45ish minutes, I'll run through the agenda then Diego will walk through the burst sim plan.
00:12 Priya Patel: great, thanks Sara. quick reminder we had the 95th latency target of sub 350ms for interactive features, right?
00:20 Sara Kim: yeah that's the stated SLO, and the pilot, the pilot has been hitting it on average but the concern is tail under burst.
00:28 Marcus Green: uh so last week we saw a spike where p99 jumped to like 1.8 seconds during that external cron job, so we want to avoid surprises in production.
00:39 Diego Alvarez: right, and that's exactly what the burst sim is intended to reproduce — we do a controlled 10x ramp for 60 seconds with varying seq lengths so we can see warm pool evaporation, kv cache misses, and cold start behavior.
00:52 Eloise Tan: quick Q, when you say warm pool evaporation, do you mean instances being scaled down because of scale-to-zero or something else?
00:58 Diego Alvarez: good question. yeah, by "evaporation" I mean autoscaler shrinkage plus GPU spin-down and then the time to rehydrate the model state. on Dedicated we have a warm-pool option where we keep N GPUs hot for short windows, that reduces rehydrate time but costs more.
01:12 Tom O'Riley: is the warm-pool a feature that keeps KV cache in memory or just the model process? because our workload is prefix-heavy so kv cache hit-rate matters a lot.
01:21 Diego Alvarez: warm-pool keeps the model process live and the KV cache active for pinned sessions; however, there are nuances — if the request comes to a different shard or model variant the cache won't help. the simulation will include a pattern to quantify effective cache hit uplift.
01:36 Priya Patel: okay, and what about the autoscale policy settings — we currently have target cpu at 60% and scale cool-down 120s in our mock?
01:44 Diego Alvarez: we're proposing conservative defaults for the POC: target utilization 40-50% for headroom, min replica pool of 2 gpus per shard, scale-out evaluation window 30s, scale-in cooldown 300s to avoid immediate shrink during short bursts.
01:58 Marcus Green: 300s is long, that could increase cost substantially if we keep GPUs idle, any mitigations?
02:04 Sara Kim: that's why we test warm-pool + short-term burst credit. the idea: keep a small warm pool (1 extra node per shard) and use burst borrowing to cover the first 90s where most tail happens, then autoscaler brings up more nodes as sustained load persists.
02:20 Priya Patel: can you explain burst borrowing again? I think our infra team called it pre-warm credit in their notes.
02:25 Diego Alvarez: sure — burst borrowing is the Dedicated feature that lets you exceed the committed pool temporarily by using a reserved burst capacity. it's billed at a premium but avoids cold-start latency. think of it as short-term oversubscribe.
02:36 Marcus Green: how do we actually trigger it? is it automatic or do we have to flip a policy?
02:41 Diego Alvarez: automatic by default if you enable the burst policy; policies can be configured by percent over baseline and maximum burst duration per hour. we'll share the policy schema after the call.
02:51 Eloise Tan: and if the burst capacity is exhausted and the autoscaler hasn't fully scaled, do you fall back to a smaller quantized model?
02:58 Diego Alvarez: yes, that's our recommended fallback chain: primary model -> quantized variant (4-bit) -> lightweight reranker for top-k. each step reduces token cost and latency at the expense of some quality. we'll measure quality delta in your eval suite.
03:12 Priya Patel: hm quality delta, our product team will need those numbers. Eloise: can you own ingesting the eval set?
03:18 Eloise Tan: yeah I can do that, I'll load the current prompts and label counts and we can run the same harvest tests.
03:24 Tom O'Riley: question on observability — we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route latency dashboards, is that already exported to our Datadog?
03:31 Sara Kim: yes, Redwood Console can emit per-route metrics and we have an exporter for Datadog. Diego will hook the token-cost breakdown stream to your account in the sandbox.
03:39 Diego Alvarez: I'll open the export during the sim and share the dashboard link. expect per-token breakouts and KV cache hit heatmaps.
03:45 Priya Patel: excellent. one more thing — security/compliance: our legal wants to see SOC2 statements and audit log formats if we enable Dedicated, can you send those?
03:54 Sara Kim: yep, we'll attach the SOC2 report and audit log sample to the thread after the call.
03:58 Marcus Green: ok back to sizing — what size GPU do you recommend for our 95-percentile 1k token prompt mixes?
04:06 Diego Alvarez: based on your current throughput, we recommend A100-40GB or H100-80GB quant-friendly configs depending on your sequence length distribution. longer sequences favor H100 for memory headroom; shorter many small requests better utilize smaller memory with more parallel contexts.
04:23 Tom O'Riley: we have limited budget, would a mixed pool help? like keep cheaper instances for baseline and switch heavier ones only on sustained high tail?
04:31 Diego Alvarez: absolutely, mixed pools are a primary pattern we see — route short requests to smaller, cheaper instances and route high-seq requests to a heavy-weight shard. smart routing can be per-route or per-request based on token estimate.
04:43 Priya Patel: what about rollout/fallback policies in case the quantized model regresses? we need canary thresholds and automatic revert.
04:50 Sara Kim: Redwood supports canary rollouts with auto-metrics gating — if latency improves but quality drops beyond threshold X we revert. Diego will propose thresholds; usually teams set a quality delta limit at 1-2% for production canaries.
05:02 Eloise Tan: do you have examples of those thresholds? our legal wants to make sure we don't accidentally degrade user experience.
05:09 Diego Alvarez: yes I'll share a template: canary size 5% traffic, monitor latency p95/p99, monitor quality via eval probes every minute, auto-revert if quality drop exceeds 1.5% for 10 minutes.
05:23 Priya Patel: sounds good. about the sim itself, what's the exact plan and timeline?
05:28 Diego Alvarez: plan: 1) ingest your real traffic histogram (we'll replay to match 50/90/99 percentiles), 2) run a 10x burst for 60s then hold at 3x for 5 minutes, 3) run a warm-pool-enabled variant and compare, 4) repeat with fallback chain enabled. estimated run time 45m, then 24h of log collection for post-analysis.
05:49 Marcus Green: will the sim hit our VPC endpoint? we don't want green traffic leaking to prod.
05:54 Diego Alvarez: it will run against a sandbox Dedicated cluster in your VPC stub — no prod access, no data storage beyond logs you opt into. we'll provide the stub endpoint and credentials.
06:05 Tom O'Riley: any chance the burst sim will accidentally trigger our autoscaling elsewhere? we have infra hooks based on GPU consumption alarms.
06:11 Diego Alvarez: we'll run the sim with a tagging header so your infra alarms can filter; we can also run with a dry-run flag that emits metrics but doesn't touch some of your downstream alarms.
06:20 Priya Patel: ok noted. cost projection — can we get an estimate of worst-case hourly during burst so finance can sign off?
06:26 Sara Kim: yes, Diego will export a per-minute cost model including burst premium; we'll include both engineered worst-case and expected median.
06:33 Diego Alvarez: expect the burst premium to be roughly 2.5x the committed rate for minutes where burst is active; warm-pool increases baseline cost by about 12-18% depending on pool size. we'll give a few scenarios.
06:47 Eloise Tan: that premium seems high but better than p99 outages. product prefers graceful degradation over high latency.
06:54 Marcus Green: final-ish question: how does KV cache rebalance when you scale horizontally? I assume some misses on redistribution?
07:01 Diego Alvarez: yes, if you shard by session we can reduce cross-shard misses; we also provide a cache repop strategy that warms cache for expected prefixes post-scale. the sim includes a step to measure miss rate and rewarm time.
07:16 Priya Patel: excellent. any blockers from Redwood side?
07:19 Sara Kim: none, Diego has the scripts ready; we just need your traffic histogram and a sandbox VPC.
07:24 Priya Patel: I'll coordinate with Marcus and Tom to export histograms.
07:29 Marcus Green: I'll also raise a ticket with infra to allow the tagging header and ensure alarms are suppressed for sim.
07:34 Sara Kim: perfect. Recap: Redwood runs burst sim and shares dashboards + cost model; BlueRiver sends histograms; schedule final review next week.
07:44 Priya Patel: thanks all. Diego, any last notes?
07:47 Diego Alvarez: just one small thing — expect noisy transcription in some logs, our agent might mis-label acronyms like V P C as V P C, so don't be surprised if the exported transcripts look odd. [laughter]
07:58 Sara Kim: cool, we'll follow up in the thread with links and the policy schema. thanks everyone.
08:03 Meeting end.

Post-call notes: Redwood to attach POC policy schema, SOC2 link, and a small readme about warm-pool vs scale cooldown tradeoffs. Logs and sim artifacts will be stored under the deal folder CRM-74822.
